document.executive_summary: All four compute node packages clear both client gates, so ranking turns entirely on measured energy. On the shared acceptance-batch basis, P3 draws 10 Wh — the lowest — followed by P2 at 22 Wh (+12), P1 at 28 Wh (+18) and P4 at 49 Wh (+39). Under the strict minimize-energy policy the recommendation is P3. Two margins need attention: P3 carries 4 of the 5 permitted defects, one step from disqualification, with P2 (22 Wh, zero defects) the natural fallback; and P1's quality index of 87 sits only 7 points above the floor. Cost, delivery, maintenance and field reliability remain unverified and cannot enter the ranking; carried as open questions for verification.
document.figure_caption: WO-03 handover diagram: gate panel (quality ≥80, defects ≤5, all pass), energy ladder with gaps +12/+18/+39 Wh above P3's 10 Wh minimum, and the decision flow to the selected package.

recommendation.rationale: P3 is the client winner: all gates pass, its 10 Wh measured energy is the lowest, and it sits 12 Wh below runner-up P2 on the identical acceptance-batch basis. The strict minimize-energy policy selects it outright. P3's 4/5 defect ceiling is a monitored contingency with P2 (22 Wh, zero defects) as fallback — a risk note, not an override.

sections.body: The policy admits a package only if quality is at least 80 and raw defects are at most 5. All four pass: quality P4 98, P3 97, P2 95, P1 87; defects P1 0, P2 0, P4 2, P3 4. With nobody excluded, selection reduces to lowest measured energy, tie-broken by lowest candidate ID. Energy ranks P3 10 Wh, P2 22, P1 28 and P4 49, so no tie-break is needed. P3 leads P2 by 12 Wh; P4 trails by 39 Wh, the widest gap in the register, so its best-in-set quality of 98 cannot offset the energy penalty.
sections.heading: Eligibility gates and energy ranking

sections.body: Every measurement shares one fixed workload, output requirement and test basis, so gaps compare directly: +12 (P2), +18 (P1) and +39 Wh (P4) above the 10 Wh minimum. Consecutive spacing is 12, 6 and 21 Wh — non-uniform, with a tight P2–P1 cluster and a wide P1–P4 tail. P2 costs 2.2× the minimum energy; P4 costs 4.9×. If the client ever weighted quality, P4's 98 index would matter, but the stated policy is energy-first with no quality tie-break, so quality differences here are informational only. Any cross-round comparison should first confirm the batch and load remain identical.
sections.heading: Energy gaps on the shared basis

sections.body: P3 qualifies with 4 raw defects against a ceiling of 5 — zero margin. A regrade adding two or more defects disqualifies P3 and moves the win to P2 at 22 Wh (zero defects, 15-point quality margin). P4 holds 2 defects and 98 quality but 49 Wh, so even a clean regrade cannot lift it into contention under the energy rule. P1's 87 quality carries a 7-point margin, and P2's zero-defect record is the most regrade-robust. Verification should test P3's defect count first — the single most decision-relevant uncertainty; all other packages' status is stable under plausible regrades.
sections.heading: Risk margins and regrade sensitivity

sections.body: Cost, delivery, maintenance and field reliability are not supplied and stay unverified; none may enter today's ranking. Open questions: (1) is P3's 4-defect count stable, given its zero ceiling margin; (2) does the shared acceptance-batch basis hold across future work orders, or should rounds re-baseline; (3) will cost or delivery evidence arrive that could justify departing from the strict energy rule — any such change must come from the client; (4) bound measurement uncertainty on the 10 Wh figure. Per the round-2 handover, every figure above traces to the trusted table.
sections.heading: Unverified factors and open questions
